statement: In healthy young adults at a German university who drank beer and white wine under medical supervision to the same level of intoxication, drinking beer before wine compared with wine before beer (each person tried both orders in a randomized crossover trial) does not detectably change next-day hangover severity: the difference between groups was −0.68 points on the 0 to 56 Acute Hangover Scale (P = 0.71; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 3.0), which rules out a difference as large as the 8 points the trial was planned to detect but not a smaller one; participants who drank only beer or only wine on different days did not differ either (Köchling et al., 2019). In exploratory analyses, vomiting and feeling very drunk went with worse hangovers, and women reported worse hangovers than men, although the paper's Discussion says it found no difference between women and men. The trial used one lager and one white wine, was open-label and analysed only completers (90 of 105). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, the order of beer and wine made no detectable difference to the next day's hangover: beer before wine and wine before beer felt about the same. What went with worse hangovers was vomiting and feeling very drunk.
population: 90 healthy adults aged 19 to 40 (half women) at a German university, excluding people of East Asian origin, who completed both sessions
exposure: Beer then white wine in one session, drunk to a set level of intoxication under medical supervision (drinks and amounts are on the study card)
comparator: The same people drinking wine then beer in another session; in a control group, beer only against wine only on different days
outcome: Next-day Acute Hangover Scale score (eight symptoms, 0 to 56)
magnitude: Within-person difference between orders: −0.32 (SD 7.63) in the group that drank beer then wine first against 0.36 (SD 6.82) in the group that drank wine then beer first, P = 0.71; editors' approximate 95% CI for the difference −4.4 to 3.0 points; planned meaningful difference 8 points (14% of the scale). Control group: no difference between beer-only and wine-only days (P > 0.05). Women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009; data not shown).

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity; Figure 3
evidence.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: The within-person difference in hangover score between drinking orders was −0.32 (SD 7.63) in study group 1 and 0.36 (SD 6.82) in study group 2 (31 each), P = 0.71; none of the three groups had a significantly different score with a different order or drink, including controls drinking beer only on one day and wine only on the other.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Sample size; Results › Study population
evidence.locator: Methods › Sample size; Results › Study population, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The trial was planned to detect a 14% difference (1 point on each of 8 items) with 80% power, targeting 36 per study group; 105 were randomized and 90 completed (31, 31 and 28), losses being mostly due to exams or holidays.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity; Figure 5
evidence.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 5 legend
evidence.extracted: In exploratory regressions with backward selection, vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher hangover scores on both days; women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009), a tendency that remained, not significantly, after dividing by peak breath alcohol.
The authors note that only a lager and a white wine were used, that blinding beer and wine proved impossible, and that an alcohol-free control group was not feasible.

risk_of_bias.note: Open label with self-rated hangover, completers only (14% lost, with whole matched triplets excluded), and only retrospective public registration.

indirectness.note: The claim names the drinks, the supervised setting and the population studied.

imprecision.note: One trial with 62 people in the primary comparison; the interval excludes the planned 8-point difference but not differences of a few points.

grade.reasoning: A randomized crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low. 'Does not detectably change' is used because the interval (editors' calculation) excludes the difference the trial was designed to detect; smaller differences remain possible and the claim says so. The exploratory associations with vomiting and drunkenness are reported as associations, not as causes. Single study.
